I edited my comment with other suggestions, I don't think that book is actually the best one to start with.

Film Art: An Introduction by Bordwell and Thompson is the most popular texts for introductory film classes.

For a deeper dive, check out History Of Narrative Film by David Cook.  It's the definitive textbook on film history.  It does a great job of illuminating the great films/filmmakers/film movements while giving context to how cinema has evolved throughout the world.  It's obviously not a sit-down kind of read but makes a great reference work if you approach it one chapter at a time.  

You can browse/read it for free here: https://archive.org/details/a-history-of-narrative-film-by-david-a.-cook/page/255/mode/2up
Is there a *film* about how to read a film?

Ooh! I know this one -

Ways of Seeing by John Berger. I had to read and watch it in film school.

I can't think of any other films like this but I have to fill up the required number of characters to make my comment show up. I think that this rule could be replaced by better moderation so people don't have to put in a bunch of *Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua. Ut enim ad minim veniam, quis nostrud exercitation ullamco laboris nisi ut aliquip ex ea commodo consequat. Duis aute irure dolor in reprehenderit in voluptate velit esse cillum dolore eu fugiat nulla pariatur. Excepteur sint occaecat cupidatat non proident, sunt in culpa qui officia deserunt mollit anim id est laborum.*

Such a waste of space.

But the Berger book and film(s) are great if you can find them.

On the other side, How to Watch a Movie by David Thomson is very short, readable and accessible, although obviously suffers from a lack of depth. But it is very good, and probably well suited to the 'average MCU watcher' audience that OP mentions.
Would also highly recommend *Film as Film* by V.F. Perkins.
I thought that James Monaco book was pretty good. It's literally used as a textbook in film classes.

A really accessible intro to film theory and practice is Thomas Flight's channel on YouTube, he's particularly good on the interface between technical aspects and artistic intent. 

As with all film critics his opinions may be challenged, but his understanding of cinema on the level of editing, sound and cinematography are excellent.

His playlist on film available here 

[https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLXJ3434wIyxM8ZWct-wa-JI-ej5yMDTMO](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLXJ3434wIyxM8ZWct-wa-JI-ej5yMDTMO)

His companion Tom van der Leyden is very good on narrative and story, not in the technical boring sense that is so common in the "plot-points Robert McKee" school of analysis, but in the more emotional-humanistic sense. 

This playlist of videos on filmmaker philosophies and story is bloody brilliant.

[https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLNwwHxpB-dky5g59ly8qzqeei2NjLaXBP](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLNwwHxpB-dky5g59ly8qzqeei2NjLaXBP)

 All this stuff is very accessible, and then they have a great podcast where they get together and chat in a very informed and accessible manner.

[https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLtZRS10dC2tp2fnith-qyZcMT1AWjNauL](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLtZRS10dC2tp2fnith-qyZcMT1AWjNauL)

I know you asked for books, but in my opinion there are few books with as good a series of insights as available in these video essays and discussions. And after all film is a visual medium so videos are very convenient for discussing it.

📚 CLOSELY WATCHED FILMS: AN INTRODUCTION TO THE ART OF NARRATIVE FILM TECHNIQUE
Marilyn Fabe
🌐 English

I have been searching for a text for an Intro to Motion Pictures class and this might be it. I have dozens of other texts which are usually expensive and which attempt to cover everything. This text restrains its focus and in doing so becomes very useful to new readers about cinema. It has a great blend of comment about major theories coupled with specific examples from films. The "key event" structure spans the silent years to Mike Figgis and Timecode. There are many books which might be in a comprehensive film library, but if you are looking for an insightful guided tour of cinema art, I would choose Closely Watched Films.
